intro: Salzburg's baroque gardens get the postcards, but most of its oldest protected trees stand on ordinary ground: a farm oak once used to fatten pigs, a riverside poplar from a vanished floodplain forest, an oak and two limes on plain Riedenburg streets, a plane and a black pine that outlasted the grand hotel whose park they once grew in. The Naturdenkmal register lists dozens more; these twelve, from Itzling to Morzg to the Fordhof estate and the Aigen streets south of the centre, clear the bar this pass, alongside one import, a Californian sequoia in the Mirabellgarten.
meta_description: Salzburg's oldest protected trees stand on farms and streets, not the baroque gardens. 12 trees, from a 1933 oak to survivors of a bombed hotel.
question_meta: Salzburg's oldest confirmed tree is the Stephan-Ludwig-Roth Oak in Morzg, over 200 years old, recorded in an 1817 account. Full list of 12.
question_answer: Salzburg's oldest documented tree is the Stephan-Ludwig-Roth Oak, a pedunculate oak at a woodland edge in Morzg. A source records the Transylvanian Saxon leader and pedagogue Stephan Ludwig Roth resting under it on 15 September 1817, which means it was already a landmark two centuries ago; a local blog puts its age at over 200 years today.
question_context: The oak has real urgency behind it: the same source reports a fungal infection and expects the tree to survive only about twenty more years, which makes it worth seeing sooner rather than later. Salzburg's Naturdenkmal register runs to dozens of entries, and the nine here come from five corners of the city rather than one walkable cluster, though three, an oak and two limes on separate Riedenburg streets, sit close enough to walk in one afternoon. The Erentrudishof Oak, the city's longest-protected tree (1933), stands in a working farmyard in Morzg where pigs once fattened on its acorns. A black poplar on the Josef-Mayburger-Kai promenade is one of the last traces of the riparian forest that used to line the Salzach. A plane and a black pine share a housing-estate courtyard near the main station, the only two trees left from a grand hotel's bombed-out park, and a giant sequoia stands beside a coast redwood in the formal Mirabellgarten, the only deliberately planted tree here. None of the nine carries a hard planting date; ages come from designation years, a sighting, a claim about a pair of survivors, or a visitor's tape measure, and each page says so.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Salzburg?
faq.a: The Stephan-Ludwig-Roth Oak in Morzg, whose recorded age of over 200 years comes from an account of a Transylvanian Saxon leader resting under it in 1817.

faq.q: Where are Salzburg's most remarkable trees?
faq.a: Spread across the city rather than one walk: a farm in Morzg, a riverside promenade in Itzling, three trees on separate Riedenburg streets, a housing-estate courtyard near the main station, a residential street in Maxglan, the formal Mirabellgarten in the centre, and a second cluster to the south in Aigen, Morzg and Nonntal.

faq.q: Are Salzburg's trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all twelve stand on public ground, a working farm's publicly accessible yard, or an open housing-estate courtyard, with no entrance fee.

faq.q: Why don't Salzburg's official register trees carry ages?
faq.a: The Land Salzburg Naturdenkmal register records only the year a tree was designated, not when it was planted, so a 1933 or 1963 date is a floor on the tree's age rather than the age itself.

trees.name: The Poplar of Josef-Mayburger-Kai

location.address: Josef-Mayburger-Kai riverside promenade, right bank of the Salzach near the Traklsteg footbridge, Itzling, Salzburg

trees.access: Free, on the public riverside promenade (Salzachuferweg)
trees.transport: About 2km along the Salzach riverside path from the old town; reachable by city bus toward Itzling and a short walk to the Traklsteg footbridge.
trees.story:
A whole floodplain wood once ran along this bank of the Salzach. This black poplar is one of the last pieces of it still standing.

The Land Salzburg register says exactly that in its own entry: a remnant of the Weichholzaue, the softwood riparian forest that used to line this stretch of the river. Softwood there is not a verdict on the timber. It is the word for the willows and poplars that colonise a river's wet edge, the trees that arrive first on new ground and go first when a bank is tidied. That woodland has gone from here. A paved promenade runs in its place, and the poplar stands beside it near the Traklsteg footbridge, about two kilometres downstream from the old town, with the water on one side and Itzling on the other.

The register cites a trunk circumference of over six metres, which is a figure we are passing on rather than one we measured, and Salzburg listed the tree as a natural monument, NDM00173, in 1979. It has ended up with its own category in the Wikimedia photograph archive, seven pictures of one riverside poplar, which is more attention than most trees on that promenade will ever get.

Nobody has dated it. The register carries the year of protection and nothing else, and 1979 is a floor rather than an age. If you know when this poplar went in, or you have put a tape around it yourself, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its massive trunk, over six metres round, standing alone where the old floodplain wood has been cleared. It stands on the riverside promenade near the Traklsteg footbridge.

trees.name: The Oak of Erentrudishof

location.address: Erentrudishof organic farm, Morzg, Salzburg (Wikipedia's register transcription gives Gneiserstraße 16; Wikimedia Commons gives Morzger Straße 40 for the same farmstead, run by Stift Nonnberg; discrepancy unresolved)

trees.access: Free; stands on the grounds of the Erentrudishof organic farm shop, run by Stift Nonnberg convent. Publicly accessible during farm-shop hours (Mon-Fri 9:00-18:30, Sat 9:00-12:00) with a self-service raw-milk machine open 24/7; the shop was reported closed for renovation with a stated July 2026 reopening at the time this was researched (2026-08-29), confirm it has reopened before sending a reader.
trees.transport: Southern edge of Salzburg in Morzg; reachable by city bus toward Morzg/Hellbrunn and a short walk.
trees.story:
No tree in Salzburg has been protected for longer than this one. The oak at the Erentrudishof went onto the Land Salzburg register in 1933 as NDM00019, the earliest designation on the city's whole list, with 95 square metres of ground protected around it.

The register describes a single-stemmed oak once used for Eichelmast: pigs turned out beneath it in autumn to fatten on the acorns it dropped. That is a working relationship rather than an ornamental one, and the setting has stayed working. The Erentrudishof is a farm run by the Stift Nonnberg convent, on the southern edge of the city at Morzg, with an organic shop, weekday opening hours and a self-service raw milk machine that runs around the clock. The oak stands on the yard of a place people still visit to buy milk.

Finding the address takes a moment. The register transcription puts the farm on Gneiserstraße, the photograph archive puts it on Morzger Straße, and both mean the same farmstead. Aim for the Erentrudishof by name and ignore the street. Worth checking before you go: the shop was closed for renovation with a reopening announced for July 2026.

Nobody has dated the tree. The 1933 listing says it was already worth protecting then and nothing more, which makes it a floor rather than an age. If you know when it was planted, or you have measured the trunk, tell us.

best_time.label: September and October, when the acorns that once fattened the farm pigs come down

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its single, thick stem standing over the yard of the Erentrudishof farm shop. It stands on the organic farm's grounds, run by Stift Nonnberg convent at Morzg.

trees.name: The Stephan-Ludwig-Roth Oak

location.address: Woodland edge near the tram stop toward Birkensiedlung, Morzg, Salzburg

trees.access: Free, stands at a woodland edge / roadside in Morzg, publicly accessible
trees.transport: Near the tram stop toward Birkensiedlung in Morzg, short walk.
trees.story:
On 15 September 1817 a man stopped and rested under this oak, and Salzburg has been naming the tree after him ever since.

He was Stephan Ludwig Roth, born 1796, died 1849, a teacher and later a leader of the Transylvanian Saxons. The register records the date of that rest, which is the useful part of the story: the oak was already a landmark worth stopping at two centuries ago, or nobody would have written down which tree it was. A Salzburg blog that catalogues the city's notable trees puts the age at over two hundred years, and that is as precise as anyone has been prepared to be, so it is as precise as we will be.

It became a natural monument in 1969, with 490 square metres of protected ground around it, which is a generous piece of Morzg set aside for a single tree. It stands at a woodland edge on the southern edge of the city, a short walk from the tram, on public ground and free to reach.

Go sooner rather than later. The same blog reports a fungal infection in the tree and cites an expectation that it has roughly twenty years left. It is alive and standing now. That is what the sources say today, and a tree in that condition is worth a second look from anyone who passes it: if you see the crown thinning or the trunk opening up, tell us.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its position right at the woodland edge, a short walk from the tram stop toward Birkensiedlung. It stands on the southern edge of Morzg, on public ground.

trees.name: The Linden of Körblleitengasse

location.address: Körblleitengasse, Maxglan, Salzburg (between Kleßheimer Allee and Norbert-Brüll-Straße)

trees.access: Free, roadside tree on a public residential street (Körblleitengasse)
trees.transport: Maxglan, western Salzburg; reachable by city bus, then a short walk along Körblleitengasse.
trees.story:
The register calls this a 150-year-old lime. It has been saying so since 1963, which is the year the tree was protected and, in all likelihood, the last year anybody looked at it properly. Read the figure as an assessment made more than sixty years ago rather than a fact about the tree today.

That register, kept by Land Salzburg, is the only source we have on it: NDM00069, thirty-eight square metres of protected ground on a residential lane in Maxglan, out on the western side of the city. For a tree the state went to the trouble of protecting, it has left remarkably little trace. The local history record covers the lane itself in detail, down to the terrace slope above the Glanbach that gave the street its name and the 570 metres it runs between Kleßheimer Allee and Norbert-Brüll-Straße. It never once mentions the lime standing on it.

Two open questions, and a reader on that street could settle both. The register writes the species down only as Linde, with nothing after it, so which lime this is has never actually been recorded. And nobody appears to have taped or dated the trunk since the sixties. If you live on the Körblleitengasse, or you have stood under it and looked at the leaves, tell us what you found.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime tree growing roadside on Körblleitengasse, between Kleßheimer Allee and Norbert-Brüll-Straße. It stands on this residential lane in Maxglan.

trees.name: The Giant Sequoia of the Mirabellgarten

location.address: Mirabellgarten, beside the path just before the turn to the Bastionsgarten (now a children's playground), Salzburg

trees.access: Free, the Mirabellgarten is a public baroque garden, open daily
trees.transport: Central Salzburg, Neustadt side of the Salzach; a few minutes' walk from Mirabellplatz and the old town.
trees.story:
The best measurement anyone has of this tree was taken by a geocacher with a tape measure in December 2019: just under six metres around the base. Not a survey, and the only number there is.

It is a giant sequoia, Sequoiadendron giganteum, a Californian tree standing in an Austrian baroque garden. It is not alone in that. A coast redwood grows beside it, so the pair on the right of the path, just before the turn into the Bastionsgarten, are both imports from the far side of a continent and an ocean. Neither of them arrived by accident. Somebody chose them, planted them and then let them do the one thing a formal garden is not otherwise for, which is grow upward without being cut back.

Nobody wrote down when that happened. No planting date and no age has surfaced for either tree, which leaves the sequoia the least documented thing in a garden people cross all day long. If you have found a record of when they went in, send it and it goes on the page.

Getting there is the easy part. The Mirabellgarten is public and open daily, a few minutes from Mirabellplatz, and the turn to the Bastionsgarten is now a children's playground. Our pin comes from the geocache waypoint rather than a survey mark, which in a garden this size still puts you within a few metres of the right trees.
trees.how_to_recognise: You are looking for two Californian conifers together on the right of the path, just before the turn into the Bastionsgarten. This is the giant sequoia of the pair, just under six metres round at the base.

trees.name: The Oak of Steinbruchstraße
trees.access: Free; stands on Steinbruchstraße, an ordinary public residential street in Riedenburg with pavements on both sides (confirmed via OpenStreetMap, no access restriction on the road)
trees.transport: Riedenburg district, western Salzburg; Salzburg Quartier Riedenburg tram/bus stop is a short walk away.
trees.story:
On Steinbruchstraße in Riedenburg, an oak has been growing ivy for longer than the street's newest residents have been alive. The street takes its name from a stone quarry that once cut into the nearby Rainberg, the same hillside quarried for stone that went into Salzburg Cathedral, though no record ties this particular tree to that history: it is simply the ordinary oak that happens to stand where the quarry road once ran.

Salzburg listed it as a natural monument in 1984, NDM00196, protecting 352 square metres of ground around it. The register's whole description is short: the trunk splits into several strong branches about five metres up, and ivy has climbed most of the way up it. That is what a 1984 designation buys you, a floor rather than a biography, and nobody has recorded when the tree was planted.

It stands on an ordinary residential pavement, no gate and no ticket, in the western Riedenburg district a short walk from Salzburg's centre. The most recent photograph anyone has put online of it is from 2014, over a decade old now, so if you walk past and it still looks the way the pictures show, or looks different, that itself is worth telling us. Its age, like its exact place in Riedenburg's quarry history, is an open question rather than a guess we are prepared to make.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk, splitting into several strong branches about five metres up, with ivy climbed most of the way up it. It stands on the pavement of Steinbruchstraße in Riedenburg.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.name: The Lime of Neutorstraße 30a

location.address: Neutorstraße 30a, near the junction of Neutorstraße, Hübnergasse and Leopoldskronstraße, Riedenburg, Salzburg

trees.access: Free; the register itself describes it as standing widely visible at the edge of the property, next to the Neutorstraße/Hübnergasse/Leopoldskronstraße junction, a public street corner in Riedenburg (confirmed via OpenStreetMap: ordinary public roads, no access restriction)
trees.transport: Riedenburg district, western Salzburg, at the Neutorstraße/Hübnergasse/Leopoldskronstraße junction; Salzburg Quartier Riedenburg tram/bus stop is a short walk away.
trees.story:
A lime with more than one trunk stands at a street corner in Riedenburg, visible enough that the register itself calls it out: it stands widely visible at the edge of its property, right where Neutorstraße meets Hübnergasse and Leopoldskronstraße.

That multi-stemmed shape is the whole of what the record says about it. Salzburg designated the tree a natural monument in 1987, NDM00215, protecting 240 square metres of ground, but the register carries no planting date and no species beyond "lime", so which of Europe's limes this actually is remains a question for whoever next stands under it and looks closely at the leaves.

The corner is ordinary, a residential junction in western Salzburg's Riedenburg district with pavement on every side and nothing between the street and the tree. The newest photograph anyone has published of it dates to 2014, which is old enough that a fresher one, or a firm answer on the species, would genuinely add something nobody currently has. If you know which lime this is, or have stood on that corner recently, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its multiple trunks rising from one base, visible from all sides at the property edge. It stands at the junction of Neutorstrasse, Hubnergasse and Leopoldskronstrasse, Riedenburg.

trees.name: The Lime of Gärtnerstraße

location.address: Gärtnerstraße, near the Mölckhof (Gärtnerstraße 2), Riedenburg, Salzburg

trees.access: Free; stands on/beside Gärtnerstraße, a public residential street in Riedenburg (OpenStreetMap tags the road 'access=destination', which restricts through motor traffic only, not pedestrians)
trees.transport: Riedenburg district, western Salzburg; Salzburg Quartier Riedenburg tram/bus stop is a short walk away.
trees.story:
This lime once stood inside the grounds of a baroque manor. The Mölckhof, a country house built around 1757 for the court chancellor Felix Anton von Mölck, expanded its park at some point after that, and the tree the register still describes belonged to it.

That is as far as the connection goes, and it is worth being precise about the gap: the manor's 1757 build date is well documented, but nothing ties this specific lime to that year, only to a later, undated expansion of the grounds. Guessing an age from the house would be a neater story than the evidence supports, so the tree's age stays unknown rather than borrowed from its neighbour's history. Salzburg protected it in 1991 as NDM00232, 226 square metres, and its only other recorded feature is a trunk that splits into several branches about four metres up.

The Mölckhof still stands on Gärtnerstraße in Riedenburg, and the lime is nearby on the same street, reachable on foot with nothing barring the way. The most recent photographs online are from 2014, over a decade old, so a current one would be useful. Which lime this actually is has never been recorded past the genus: if you can name the species, or know anything about when it was planted, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lime that once stood inside the grounds of the Molckhof manor house. It stands on Gartnerstrasse, near the Molckhof, Riedenburg.

trees.name: The Last Trees of the Fordhof
trees.species: London Plane (Platanus x acerifolia) and Black Pine (Pinus nigra)

location.address: Courtyard of the Fordhof housing estate, off Rainerstraße, Elisabeth-Vorstadt, Salzburg (plane tree pin; the pine stands about 35m away in the same courtyard)

trees.access: Free; the two trees stand in the open courtyard of the Fordhof, a multi-block 1953 housing estate, criss-crossed by ordinary public sidewalks between the apartment blocks (confirmed via OpenStreetMap: lit, surfaced public footways run through the courtyard; the only access=private tags nearby cover two small surface parking areas, not the walkways or the tree positions). Not a park, and worth saying so plainly: this is a residential courtyard rather than public green space, but nothing gates entry.
trees.transport: Elisabeth-Vorstadt, about 5-10 minutes' walk from Salzburg Hauptbahnhof (the main train station).
trees.story:
A grand hotel once stood where an apartment courtyard is now, and two of its trees are the only things that survived the change. The Hotel de l'Europe operated from 1865 to 1938, was bombed and stood empty until cleared around 1949, and the housing blocks of the Fordhof estate went up on the same ground in 1953. Everything about the hotel disappeared except a plane tree and a black pine, both registered as natural monuments, both still growing in what is now a residential courtyard.

The plane went onto the register in 1964, the pine in 1973, each protecting 113 square metres, and both entries say the same thing in the same words: this is one of two surviving trees from the hotel's park. That claim is the whole basis for an age. If either tree was planted right at the end of the hotel's run, it is about 88 years old; if it dates from the 1865 opening, it is 161. Nobody has narrowed that further, and neither should we.

This is the least garden-like setting on Salzburg's list: an ordinary 1953 housing estate off Rainerstraße, a short walk from the main station, with public footpaths running through the courtyard between the blocks. Nothing gates it, but it takes a moment to believe two centuries-old natural monuments are sitting in someone's car park. If you know which end of that date range is closer to true, or have measured either trunk, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its trunk standing alone in the open courtyard of the Fordhof housing estate, off Rainerstraße; the black pine grows about 35 metres away in the same courtyard.

trees.name: The Hornbeam of Freisaalweg

location.address: Freisaalweg, beside the public Parkplatz Akademiestraße car park, Nonntal, Salzburg

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_in_Salzburg (register entry NDM00202, designated 1986, protected area 0.049 ha)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freisaal (independent Wikipedia article on the Freisaal district, states the tree's estimated age directly: 'eine mehrstämmige Hainbuche, deren Alter auf mehr als 200 Jahre geschätzt wird')
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Naturdenkmal_Hainbuche_am_Freisaalweg,_Salzburg.JPG (dated, geotagged photo, 22 May 2014, coordinates match the register centroid to within a few metres)
trees.access: Free. Stands beside the public Parkplatz Akademiestraße car park (220 spaces) in Nonntal; publicly viewable, no gate or restriction found.
trees.transport: Bus line 20 (Nonntal route), stop Akademiestraße or Hofhaymer-Allee; about a 15-20 minute walk south from Salzburg's Altstadt (Residenzplatz)
trees.story:
This hornbeam is all that is left of a villa garden, and for years it was the tree outside Salzburg University's biology department. The villa on Freisaalweg dates from the Gründerzeit, the building boom around the turn of the last century, and it later housed the university's Institute of Biology until 1986, when the biologists moved to the new natural sciences building nearby.

That same year, on 23 January 1986, the city declared the hornbeam a natural monument. The register entry calls it notably symmetrical and mighty, and the local Wikipedia article on Freisaal singles out its strikingly round, globe-shaped crown. It grows on several stems rather than one trunk.

Its age is an estimate and stays one: the Freisaal article puts it at more than 200 years, and nobody has published anything sharper. No source says whether it was planted for the villa's garden or was already standing when the villa went up.

Today its neighbour is the Akademiestraße car park, 220 spaces of asphalt, an unglamorous address for a protected tree. The most recent dated sighting we found is a photograph from May 2014, so if you walk past, a new photo or a word that it still stands would help. The same goes for its girth, which no source records: a tape measure answers that in a minute. It is a 15 to 20 minute walk south of the Altstadt.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its several stems and its round, globe-shaped crown. It stands on Freisaalweg beside the Parkplatz Akademiestraße car park.

trees.name: The Courtyard Oak of Aigner Straße

location.address: Aigner Straße 9, in the courtyard behind the apartment blocks, Aigen, Salzburg

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_in_Salzburg (register entry NDM00251, designated 2005, protected area 0.033 ha, quotes the tree's own access text)

https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datei:Eiche_an_der_Aigner_Strasse_9_(1).JPG (independent dated, geotagged photo by a different photographer, 30 May 2014, coordinates match the register centroid closely, uploaded for the Wiki Loves Earth 2014 contest)
trees.access: Free and explicitly unrestricted. The register's own text states it plainly: 'Die Eiche an der Aigner Straße 9 steht im Innenhof mehrerer Wohnblocks. Sie ist trotzdem ohne Einschränkungen zugänglich' (stands in the courtyard of several apartment blocks; nevertheless it is accessible without restriction).
trees.transport: Salzburg Aigen station (Obus line 7 and S-Bahn S3), on Aigner Straße itself, a short walk to the courtyard
trees.story:
Salzburg protected this oak in 2005, and it went on the list standing in the courtyard of a block of flats. The city's own register entry anticipates the obvious question and answers it: the tree stands in the inner courtyard of several apartment blocks at Aigner Straße 9, and it is nevertheless accessible without restriction. You may walk in and look.

It is one of the more recent additions to Salzburg's list of natural monuments, and the register's description is about its build. Somewhere between 2.5 and 4 metres up, the register says, the trunk breaks into several strong limbs, rather than carrying its crown on one straight stem.

How long it has stood here, no source records. The register gives no age for any of its trees and no girth for this one, and it names the tree simply as Eiche, oak, without a species. We list it as a pedunculate oak, like the other oaks we map in Salzburg, but that is our reading rather than the register's: a photograph of a leaf or an acorn would settle it, and a tape measure around the trunk would give us a basis for estimating its age.

The most recent dated photograph we found is from May 2014. If you pass through Aigen, tell us it still stands. It is a short walk from Salzburg Aigen station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk splitting into several strong limbs between 2.5 and 4 metres up. It stands in the inner courtyard of the apartment blocks at Aigner Straße 9.

trees.name: The Meadow Oak of Buchholzhofstraße

location.address: Buchholzhofstraße, Kleingmain/Morzg, Salzburg, on the pedestrian and cycle path leading toward Hellbrunner Allee

verified_sources: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liste_der_Naturdenkm%C3%A4ler_in_Salzburg (register entry NDM00206, designated 1986, protected area 0.0346 ha)

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:00206_Eiche_an_der_Buchholzhofstra%C3%9Fe.jpg (independent dated, geotagged photo, 16 August 2014, categorised by Commons as Quercus robur, coordinates match the register centroid closely)
trees.access: Free. Stands beside Buchholzhofstraße, whose northern stretch is a public pedestrian and cycle path (Geh- und Radweg) running into the Hellbrunner Allee; no gate or restriction found.
trees.transport: Bus/Obus line 5 or bus line 25 (Morzg route); about a 20-25 minute walk south from Salzburg's Altstadt
trees.story:
This oak is protected as a leftover of a landscape that no longer exists. Salzburg's register calls it a Kulturrelikt, a cultural relic: the last trace of the open, thinly wooded meadows that once spread near the Hellbrunner Allee, before this corner of Kleingmain and Morzg was built up.

It was declared a natural monument in 1986, and the register's reason is not its size or its shape but what it remembers: the ground here was once meadow with scattered trees, and this oak is what remains of it. The street it now stands on was only named in 1941, after the Buchholzhof.

No source gives its age, and nobody has published its girth, so we will not guess. The register's framing implies it was here long before 1986, but it puts no number on that. If you have measured it, tell us, and we can at least estimate.

The species stands on firmer ground: the register says only Eiche, oak, but a geotagged photograph on Wikimedia Commons from August 2014 is filed as Quercus robur. That photograph is also the most recent sighting we found, so a word that it still stands would help. As far as we can tell the northern stretch of Buchholzhofstraße is now a footpath and cycle path running toward the Hellbrunner Allee; it is about a 20 to 25 minute walk south of the Altstadt.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone protected oak beside Buchholzhofstraße, on the footpath and cycle path that leads toward the Hellbrunner Allee in Morzg.
